title: Bidirectional BFS in Porto: Meet in the Middle!
description: Watch how Bidirectional BFS finds the shortest path by launching two BFS waves—one from the start and one from the goal—until they meet. This visualization maps the idea onto real street-grid graphs in Porto (Miragaia).
ig_caption:
🚦✨ Bidirectional BFS in Porto (Miragaia) — the shortest path “meets in the middle.”

🧠 Here’s the graph-theory idea: treat the street map as an unweighted graph (intersections = nodes, roads = edges). Instead of running BFS from just the start, we run **two BFS frontiers simultaneously**—one expanding outward from the start and one from the goal—until they intersect. ✅

🔍 Why it’s fast: BFS explores by increasing distance, so two smaller-radius searches reduce the explored space compared to a single-source BFS, especially on large graphs. When the frontiers touch, we reconstruct the route by combining the parent pointers from both directions. 🧩

📍Real-world twist: street maps aren’t perfect grids—so the visualization shows how obstacles, varying connectivity, and edge layout shape the search layers on real geometry.
